title: Live by nature
hook: Zeno's goal: live in agreement with nature (Diogenes Laërtius 7.87)

segments.voice: Yesterday: eupatheia, the good feelings the Stoics kept: joy, wise wishing, caution. Your line was joy is allowed.

Live by nature. Put those words on a label and they'll sell you almost anything. Granola. Face cream. A cabin in the woods with no wifi. Barefoot running shoes, a strange idea if you think about it. So when you hear that the founder of the Stoics said the whole point of life is to live in agreement with nature, you might picture a man in a toga hugging a tree. That's not what Zeno meant. What he meant is stranger, and more useful. We're still on the porch, now in the Stoic world.
screen: `LIVE BY NATURE, ON A LABEL.` → `NOT A TOGA HUGGING A TREE.` → `LIVE BY NATURE.`

segments.voice: Diogenes Laërtius reports that Zeno, in a book called On the Nature of Man, was the first to say the goal of life is to live in agreement with nature, and that this is the same as living by virtue. There's a small puzzle in the sources. Another ancient report says Zeno's own phrase was shorter: just live in agreement. Live consistently, all of a piece, not at war with yourself. His successors, it says, added the words with nature. Scholars still discuss which is right. Either way, the idea grew to hold two natures. The first is your own. For the Stoics, a human is an animal that reasons and lives with others. A fish lives by its nature when it swims; a human lives by hers when she thinks clearly and treats people well. Living by nature means living up to the human part of you. The second is the nature of the whole world. Chrysippus said our nature is part of the nature of everything, and the good life fits the pattern of the whole, like a note that fits a song. So, not a cabin in the woods: a Stoic could live by nature in a city office. Still, Marcus Aurelius looked closely at ordinary natural things. In one passage of his notebook he notices figs splitting open, ripe olives, the cracks on a baked loaf, a lion's brow, and says they have their own beauty because they belong to the order of things. Agreement with yourself, with others, with the whole.
screen: `ZENO: LIVE IN AGREEMENT WITH NATURE.` · `ALL OF A PIECE, NOT AT WAR.` · `YOUR NATURE: REASON AND OTHERS.` · `THE NATURE OF THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `IN AGREEMENT.`

segments.voice: If you can, face a window or step outside; if not, picture the last tree you saw. Look at one living thing, a plant, a bird, a patch of sky, simply doing what it is. Then notice your own breath doing what it does, your mind noticing: for now, you and the tree are in agreement.
Zeno. The Stoic founder who said the goal of life is to live in agreement with your own nature and the nature of the whole.
Your line: in agreement. All of a piece, inside and out, wherever you are. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism today read 'living by nature' as living up to reason and fellowship, and some make a habit of time outdoors as a reminder of the larger order.

options: no, live up to reason and fit the whole, wherever you are.
fork.reveal: for the Stoics a human lives by nature by reasoning well and living well with others, in any place.

notes: Diogenes Laërtius 7.87: Zeno, On the Nature of Man, first said the end is living in agreement with nature, i.e. according to virtue; paraphrased.
Stobaeus 2.7.6a: Zeno's formula 'to live in agreement', with Cleanthes adding 'with nature' (some reports say Chrysippus expanded it further); confirm attribution.
Meditations 3.2 (figs, olives, bread, lion's brow): paraphrased; confirm details.
Greek transliteration of the original phrase: confirm the pronunciation guide.
